To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a country fares best in an exchange-rate regime if it is subject to real shocks that originate abroad, if its labor market is indexed to current changes of the price level, and if its trade is primarily with other members within the union.

a country that is subject to real or monetary disturbances originating at its own borders or abroad is better off if it joins an exchange-rate union, provided that wages do not respond to changes in the general level of prices, and that the country is a small country and has a high degree of trade integration with other countries in the union.

the case for a monetary union is strengthened if the domestic country has an indexed wage regime, if the country trades primarily with the other members of the monetary union, and if the disturbances are primarily monetary in nature.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of disturbances in a small country that joins an exchange-rate union.
the question of whether or not a small country should fix its currency to another country or countries in order to reduce the variability of its output.
the question of whether or not the effects of disturbances are modified if the domestic economy is a member of a monetary union.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the union is not a cure-all for the small open economy.

a small country fares better in a union if disturbances originate at home, if the domestic country has a comparative advantage in goods traded with other members of a union, and if wage indexation is not very high.
the case for a fixed exchange rate regime is stronger than the case against it.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, if the union is to be a success, the members must have similar economic characteristics and the union must have the ability to respond to disturbances with appropriate policies.
a union is not a panacea for a small country, but that it is a reasonable alternative to a flexible exchange rate regime.
the case for a small country to fix the exchange rate with a large country is not strong.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the case for a currency union is not as strong as commonly believed.
the small country model, which is the most commonly used model in the literature, cannot be used to analyze the effects on the union of foreign disturbances.
the case for a fixed exchange-rate union must be made on a case-by-case basis.
